title: Girls outperform boys in school. Then the gap reverses. The HCI+ explains why
gist: World Bank HCI+ data shows women score ~5 points higher than men on health and education combined but 19 points lower overall, with employment and lost work experience accounting for essentially the entire gender gap in lifetime human capital.

themes.theme: Gender gap is a jobs gap

insights.claim: Women score about 5 HCI+ points higher than men on health and education combined, yet their total HCI+ score is 19 points lower, with employment accounting for essentially all of the difference.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Female labor-force participation, not schooling, is the lever for closing lifetime human-capital and earnings gaps in developing markets.
insights.quote: Women score about 5 HCI+ points higher than men on health and education combined. Yet their total HCI+ score is 19 points lower.
insights.locator: 1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap

insights.claim: Despite girls now outperforming boys in school across much of the world, men end up with a 21 percent advantage in expected lifetime earnings globally, driven by what happens after school rather than during it.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Education-parity metrics overstate real economic progress for women; earnings gaps persist and are structural to the labor market.
insights.quote: Yet men end up with a 21 percent advantage in expected earnings globally. The reason is almost entirely about what happens after school, not during it.

insights.claim: In South Asia, on-the-job learning alone explains 98 percent of the gender gap in human capital.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Regional policy for South Asia should target getting women into learning-rich wage jobs, not just classroom outcomes.
insights.quote: In South Asia, on-the-job learning alone explains 98 percent of the gender gap.
insights.locator: 1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap

insights.claim: In 101 of 145 countries with sex-disaggregated data, women outperform men on health and education but men have higher overall HCI+ scores once employment and work experience are counted.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The reversal is near-universal, not a handful of outliers, signaling a systemic labor-market failure to convert female education into productivity.
insights.locator: 1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap

insights.claim: A worker with 30 years of experience in a wage job is roughly two and a half times as productive as a new entrant, a gain roughly equivalent to completing 12 years of average-quality schooling.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Work experience is quantifiably a form of human-capital accumulation comparable to a full secondary education, so exclusion from work compounds over a lifetime.
insights.quote: A worker with 30 years of experience in a wage job is roughly two and a half times as productive as someone just starting out, a gain roughly equivalent to completing 12 years of average quality schooling.
insights.locator: 1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap

insights.claim: Across 151 countries roughly one in four young people is a NEET, rising to one in three in low- and middle-income countries and 41 percent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Large NEET shares represent a demographic-dividend loss and a structural drag on future productivity in emerging markets.
insights.quote: In the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan, it hits 41 percent.

insights.claim: The HCI+ estimates that each year a young person spends outside work or school depreciates their skills at a rate of about 1.25 percent, on top of the skills they fail to accumulate.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Time out of the labor market is not neutral; it actively erodes existing human capital, making early re-entry policies high-return.
insights.quote: each year outside work or school reduces skills at an estimated rate of 1.25 percent.

insights.claim: Globally 40 percent of young women aged 20-24 are neither working nor studying versus 17 percent of young men, widening to 63 versus 20 percent in the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan and 55 versus 15 percent in South Asia.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: The NEET burden is overwhelmingly female and regionally concentrated, pinpointing where female-employment interventions would move the most human capital.
insights.quote: Globally, 40 percent of young women aged 20–24 are neither working nor studying, compared to 17 percent of young men.

insights.claim: The HCI+ App's female employment deep dive identifies, country by country, whether the binding barrier is women being outside the labor force, unemployed, or in low-learning jobs, distinctions that drive different policy responses.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Diagnosing the specific barrier per country lets development policy avoid one-size-fits-all female-employment programs.
insights.locator: 1. The gender gap in human capital is a jobs gap

insights.claim: A revamped HCI+ simulation tool lets users isolate a single driver such as employment and see its projected effect on future earnings, allowing a policymaker to model outcomes like bringing more young women into wage employment or cutting the NEET rate by ten percentage points.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
insights.so_what: Quantified, country-level counterfactuals turn human-capital diagnosis into concrete policy simulations governments can act on.
insights.quote: what happens to our economy if we bring more young women into wage employment?
